title: Knowledge of God is a gift of grace
source_text: Κέλσος μὲν οὖν ἤτοι τῇ συνθέσει τῇ ἐπὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἀνάλογον τῇ παρὰ τοῖς γεωμέτραις καλουμένῃ συνθέσει ἢ τῇ ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἀναλύσει ἢ καὶ ἀναλο γίᾳ ἀνάλογον τῇ παρὰ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀναλογίᾳ οἴεται γινώσκεσθαι τὸν θεὸν, ἐπὶ τὰ πρόθυρα εἰ ἄρα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ δυναμένου τινὸς οὕτως ἐλθεῖν· ὁ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος εἰπών· „οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ“ θείᾳ τινὶ χάριτι, οὐκ ἀθεεὶ ἐγγινομένῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἀλλὰ μετά τινος ἐνθουσιασμοῦ. ἀποφαίνεται γινώσκεσθαι τὸν θεόν. καὶ γὰρ εἰκὸς μείζονα μὲν ἢ κατὰ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν εἶναι τὴν γνῶσιν τοῦ θεοῦ (διὸ καὶ τὰ τοσαῦτα παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις ἐστὶ περὶ θεοῦ σφάλματα) χρηστότητι δὲ καὶ φιλανθρωπίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ παραδόξῳ καὶ θειοτέρᾳ χάριτι φθάνειν τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ γνῶσιν ἐπὶ τοὺς προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ προκαταληφθέντας ὅτι ἀξίως βιώσουσι τοῦ ἐγνωσμένου, οὐδαμῶς παραχαράττοντες τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν εὐσέβειαν, οὔτε ἂν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγνοούντων ὅ τι ποτέ ἐστιν εὐσέβεια καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι ποτ᾿ οὖν μᾶλλον ἀναπλαττόντων εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν ἢ ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἡ εὐσέβεια τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ ἀπάγωνται, οὔτε ἂν καταγελαστότατοι εἶναι νομίζωνται. ὁρῶν δ᾿ οἶμαι ὁ θεὸς καὶ τὴν ἀλαζονείαν ἢ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς ἄλλους ὑπεροψίαν τῶν μεγάλα μὲν φρονούντων ἐπὶ τῷ ἐγνωκέναι τὸν θεὸν καὶ ἀπὸ φιλοσοφίας τὰ θεῖα μεμαθηκέναι παραπλησίως δὲ τοῖς ἀπαιδευτοτάτοις ἐπὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα καὶ τοὺς νεὼς αὐτῶν καὶ τὰ θρυλούμενα μυστήρια ἀγόντων „ἐξελέξατο“ „τὰ μωρὰ τοῦ κόσμου,“ τοὺς ἐν Χριστιανοῖς ἁπλουστάτους καὶ πολλῶν φιλοσόφων μετριώτερον καὶ καθαρώτερον βιοῦντας, „ἵνα καταισχύνῃ τοὺς σοφοὺς,“ οὐκ αἰδουμένους ἐν τῷ τοῖς ἀψύχοις προσομιλεῖν ὡς θεοῖς ἢ θεῶν εἰκόσιν. τίς γὰρ νοῦν ἔχων οὐ καταγελάσεται τοῦ μετὰ τοὺς τηλικούτους καὶ τοσούτους ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ περὶ θεοῦ ἢ θεῶν λόγους ἐνορῶντος τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν καὶ ἤτοι αὐτοῖς ἀναπέμποντος τὴν εὐχὴν ἢ διὰ τῆς τούτων ὄψεως ἐφ᾿ ὃν φαντάζεται δεῖν ἀναβαίνειν ἀπὸ τοῦ βλεπομένου καὶ συμβόλου ὄντος ἀναφέροντός γε ἐπὶ τὸν νοούμενον; Χριστιανὸς δὲ καὶ ὁ ἰδιώτης πάντα μὲν τόπον τοῦ κόσμου πέπεισται εἶναι μέρος τοῦ ὅλου, ναοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ὄντος τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου· „ἐν παντὶ“ δὲ „τόπῳ“ εὐχόμενος, μύσας τοὺς τῆς αἰσθήσεως ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ ἐγείρας τοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς, ὑπεραναβαίνει τὸν ὅλον κόσμον. καὶ οὐδ᾿ ἐπὶ τὴν ἁψῖδα ἵσταται τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ εἰς τὸν ὑπερουράνιον γενόμενος τῇ διανοίᾳ τόπον, ὁδηγούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ θείου πνεύματος καὶ ὡσπερεὶ ἔξω τοῦ κόσμου τυγχάνων ἀναπέμπει οὐ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τὴν εὐχὴν τῷ θεῷ· ἔμαθε γὰρ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μηδὲν μικρὸν, τουτέστιν αἰσθητὸν, ζητεῖν ἀλλὰ μόνα τὰ μεγάλα καὶ ἀληθῶς θεῖα, οσα συμβάλλεται διδόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς τὸ ὁδεῦσαι ἐπὶ τὴν παρ᾿ αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου ὄντος θεοῦ μακαριότητα.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus then thinks God to be known (γινώσκω) either by the synthesis (σύνθεσις) onto other things, analogous to that called synthesis among geometers (γεωμέτρης), or by analysis (ἀνάλυσις) from the others, or also by analogy (ἀναλογία) analogous to the analogy among the same, if indeed one is able thus to come to the vestibule (πρόθυρα) of the Good (τὸ ἀγαθόν); but the Word of God, having said: "no one has known the Father except the Son and to whom the Son reveals (ἀποκαλύπτω)", declares (ἀποφαίνομαι) God to be known by some divine grace (θεία χάρις), coming to be in (ἐγγίνομαι) the soul not without God (ἀθεεί) but with some inspiration (ἐνθουσιασμός). For indeed it is likely (εἰκός) the knowledge (γνῶσις) of God to be greater than according to human nature (hence so many errors (σφάλμα) among men about God), but by goodness (χρηστότης) and love of mankind (φιλανθρωπία) of God and by wonderful (παράδοξος) and more divine grace the knowledge of God to reach (φθάνω) those taken beforehand (προκαταλαμβάνω) by the foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) of God that they will live worthily of the one known, in no way counterfeiting/debasing (παραχαράσσω) the piety (εὐσέβεια) toward him, neither if they should be led away (ἀπάγω) to death by those ignorant of whatever piety is and fabricating (ἀναπλάσσω) anything whatever to be piety rather than what piety is, nor if they should be thought most ridiculous (καταγέλαστος). And God, I think, seeing the boastfulness (ἀλαζονεία) or the contempt (ὑπεροψία) toward others of those thinking great things (μέγα φρονέω) on having known God and having learned divine things from philosophy, but like the most uneducated (ἀπαίδευτος) going/leading (ἄγω) to the statues (ἄγαλμα) and their temples (νεώς) and the much-talked-of (θρυλέω) mysteries, "chose (ἐκλέγομαι) the foolish (μωρός) things of the world", the simplest (ἁπλοῦς) among Christians and living more moderately (μέτριος) and more purely than many philosophers, "that he might shame (καταισχύνω) the wise", not being ashamed (αἰδέομαι) in conversing (προσομιλέω) with lifeless things (ἄψυχος) as gods or images (εἰκών) of gods. For who having sense will not laugh at (καταγελάω) the one who after so great and so many discourses in philosophy about God or gods gazes (ἐνοράω) at the statues and either sends up (ἀναπέμπω) the prayer (εὐχή) to them or through the sight (ὄψις) of them, to whom he imagines (φαντάζομαι) he must ascend (ἀναβαίνω), refers (ἀναφέρω) from the thing seen and being a symbol (σύμβολον) to the one conceived by mind (νοούμενος)? But a Christian, even the unlearned (ἰδιώτης), is persuaded every place (τόπος) of the world (κόσμος) to be a part of the whole, the whole world being a temple (ναός) of God; and praying "in every place", having closed (μύω) the eyes of sense (αἴσθησις) and raised (ἐγείρω) those of the soul, he goes up beyond (ὑπεραναβαίνω) the whole world. And he does not even stand on the vault (ἁψίς) of heaven, but coming in thought (διάνοια) into the place above heaven (ὑπερουράνιος τόπος), being guided (ὁδηγέω) by the divine Spirit (θεῖον πνεῦμα) and as it were being outside the world, he sends up the prayer to God not about ordinary things (τὰ τυχόντα); for he learned from Jesus to seek nothing small (μικρός), that is, sensible (αἰσθητός), but only the great and truly divine things, which being given by God contribute (συμβάλλομαι) toward journeying (ὁδεύω) to the blessedness (μακαριότης) with him through his Son, being the Word (λόγος), God.
pass_b_english: Celsus, then, thinks that God is known either by synthesis applied to other things, like what geometers call synthesis, or by analysis from other things, or else by analogy, like the analogy the same geometers use; if, that is, anyone can come in this way to the threshold of the Good (Plato, Philebus 64c). But the Word of God, who said, “No one has known the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son reveals him” (Matthew 11:27), declares that God is known by a divine grace, which comes to be in the soul not without God, but with a kind of inspiration.

For it is likely that the knowledge of God is greater than human nature can reach, which is why there are so many errors among men about God; but that, by the goodness and love for mankind of God, and by a wonderful and more divine grace, the knowledge of God reaches those whom God, in his foreknowledge, has laid hold of beforehand as people who would live worthily of him whom they have come to know. They would never debase their piety toward him, not even if they were led away to death by those who do not know what piety is, and who make anything at all out to be piety rather than what piety really is; nor even if they were thought to be the most ridiculous of men.

God, I think, also saw the arrogance, or the contempt for others, of those who pride themselves on having known God and on having learned divine things from philosophy, yet who, like the most ignorant, turn to statues and their temples and the much-talked-of mysteries. And so he “chose the foolish things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), the simplest among Christians, who live more temperately and more purely than many philosophers, “to put to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27), who are not ashamed to converse with lifeless things as with gods or images of gods.

For who that has sense will not laugh at a man who, after all the great and numerous discourses in philosophy about God or gods, gazes at statues, and either sends up his prayer to them, or, through the sight of them, carries it up from what is seen, which is a symbol, to the being known by the mind, to whom he fancies he must ascend? But the Christian, even the unlearned one, is convinced that every place in the world is a part of the whole, since the whole world is God’s temple. Praying “in every place” (1 Timothy 2:8), and closing the eyes of sense and raising those of the soul, he rises above the whole world.

He does not even stop at the vault of heaven, but, coming in thought to the place above the heavens (Plato, Phaedrus 247b-c), led by the divine Spirit, and being as it were outside the world, he sends up to God a prayer that is not about ordinary things. For he has learned from Jesus to seek nothing small, that is, nothing that the senses perceive, but only the great and truly divine things (compare Matthew 6:33), which, given by God, help a man on his way to the blessedness that is with him, through his Son, who is the Word and God.

choices.choice: “No one has known the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son reveals him” is Origen’s free form of Matthew 11:27 (compare Luke 10:22); he has ἔγνω and ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ for the Gospel’s ἐπιγινώσκει and ᾧ ἐὰν βούληται ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι. “the threshold of the Good” (ἐπὶ τὰ πρόθυρα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ) echoes Plato, Philebus 64c (τοῖς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ προθύροις). “the vault of heaven” (ἁψῖδα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) and “the place above the heavens” (ὑπερουράνιον τόπον) echo Plato, Phaedrus 247b-c; cited together. “in every place” cites 1 Timothy 2:8 (προσεύχεσθαι ... ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ); compare Malachi 1:11. “seek nothing small ... but only the great” reflects the saying Origen elsewhere quotes as Jesus’ (“Ask for the great things, and the small will be added to you”, De oratione 2.2), an unwritten saying; Matthew 6:33 is cited as the nearest canonical text. προγνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ προκαταληφθέντας may echo Romans 8:29 / 1 Peter 1:2, but there is no verbal quotation; left uncited. ἀθεεί: “not without God”. ἀγόντων (going/leading to the images) taken intransitively, “turn to”. τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ ἀπάγωνται: “led away to death” (ellipsis of ὁδόν). Source spacing “ἀναλο γίᾳ” read as ἀναλογίᾳ; “οσα” read as ὅσα. λόγου ὄντος θεοῦ: “who is the Word and God” (both predicates kept). Review: Philebus 64c (τοῖς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ προθύροις) and Phaedrus 247b-c (ὑπουράνιον ἁψῖδα, ὑπερουράνιον τόπον) confirmed. Matthew 6:33 does not itself speak of ‘great’ and ‘small’ things, so it is now marked “compare”. The being the image-worshipper ascends to (τὸν νοούμενον) is his own imagined deity, so lower case.
ὅτι after προκαταληφθέντας: 'because they would live' -> 'as people who would live'
'the arrogance and the contempt' -> 'the arrogance, or the contempt' (ἤ)
ἀγάλματα: 'images' -> 'statues', matching the rest of the passage
'the One known by the mind' -> 'the being known by the mind' (pagan's imagined god, not God)
Matthew 6:33 -> 'compare Matthew 6:33' (the verse does not say 'seek great things'); 'help us' -> 'help a man' (no first person in the Greek)
Matthew 11:27, 1 Corinthians 1:27, 1 Timothy 2:8, Philebus 64c, Phaedrus 247b-c checked
